items.questionAndWhy: Can educational technologies, including AI, improve learners’ ability to plan, monitor, and evaluate their own thinking? This matters because students may feel more reflective without demonstrating better regulation during actual tasks.
items.whatTheyDid: Yuan and Du synthesized 33 experimental or quasi-experimental studies using a three-level meta-analysis of 94 effect sizes. They separated metacognitive processes, technology types, instructional guidance, feedback timing, and learner control, and examined measurement and risk of bias.
items.whatTheyFound: The pooled effect favored technology-supported interventions (Hedges’ g = 0.653, 95% CI 0.520–0.786), but effects were heterogeneous. Technology type did not significantly moderate the result. Apparent advantages for guidance, immediate feedback, and system control did not survive multiple-testing correction. Ninety of 94 effects used self-report measures.
items.whatItMeans: Technology may support metacognitive regulation, but this literature mostly measures what learners report doing, not whether they actually calibrate judgments or change strategies. A PSYWERX learning tool should independently test monitoring accuracy, transfer, and behavior rather than rely only on self-report.
items.streamTitle: Technology-supported learning improved reported metacognition, but most evidence was self-report
items.streamSummary: A three-level meta-analysis of 33 studies found higher reported metacognitive outcomes following technology-supported learning interventions (Hedges’ g = 0.653). However, results varied considerably, technology type did not explain the differences, and exploratory advantages for immediate feedback or instructional guidance were not significant after multiple-testing correction. Most important, 90 of 94 effect sizes came from self-report measures. The evidence supports a promising educational role for technology, but does not establish equivalent improvements in actual monitoring, strategy use, or independent learning.

items.questionAndWhy: Is a personality trait reflected in shared patterns of brain activity, and does the surrounding situation change that relationship? A trait may become most visible when the environment makes it relevant.
items.whatTheyDid: Popp and colleagues compared personality scores and fMRI responses from 174 Human Connectome Project participants watching movies. They used inter-subject representational similarity analysis and independent ratings from 86 people to classify scenes as relevant or irrelevant to neuroticism.
items.whatTheyFound: Higher neuroticism was associated with greater between-person variability in neural responses, especially during trait-relevant scenes. The finding was not one common neural signature shared by people high in the trait; their responses were less similar. The observational association does not establish why these patterns emerged or support individual diagnosis.
items.whatItMeans: Context can change how useful a psychological trait is for interpreting observed behavior or physiology. Analysts should not assume a fixed trait has one invariant neural or behavioral marker across situations.
items.streamTitle: Personality-relevant movie scenes revealed more diverse brain responses among people high in neuroticism
items.streamSummary: An fMRI study of 174 people watching movies found that higher neuroticism was associated with more variable brain responses across individuals, particularly during scenes independently rated as relevant to the trait. Rather than identifying one uniform neural signature of neuroticism, the study found greater heterogeneity. The work supports the view that personality expression depends partly on situational context, but these are correlational group-level analyses. They do not explain the mechanism, establish clinical prediction, or justify inferring an individual’s personality from one brain scan.

items.questionAndWhy: When strangers must choose where to move under ambiguous conditions, does speaking produce faster consensus? Crowd behavior is often described as contagion even though communication and group size may act differently.
items.whatTheyDid: Konya conducted a physical crowd experiment with 444 participants in groups of roughly 10 or 24–41. They chose between apparently similar marked areas, sometimes with and sometimes without permission to communicate. Video records and group decisions were analyzed.
items.whatTheyFound: Allowing communication did not reliably change overall time to a final group arrangement. Spoken interaction could produce either homogeneous or polarized outcomes, while silent groups seldom reached complete uniformity. The intended shared-identity manipulation failed, and group-level comparisons were based on relatively few runs.
items.whatItMeans: The value is not a universal communication effect. It is a reminder to distinguish the timing, consensus, and movement stages of group behavior, and to report failed manipulations instead of interpreting them as successful tests of identity.
items.streamTitle: Communication changed the pattern of crowd decisions without shortening the time to reach them
items.streamSummary: An experiment with 444 people in small and larger anonymous crowds tested movement decisions under uncertainty, with or without verbal communication. Communication did not significantly shorten the time to reach a final arrangement. It could be associated with either strong agreement or polarization, while fully uniform outcomes were uncommon without speech. The intended shared-identity manipulation did not work, and there were too few group runs to support strong conclusions about all decision distributions. The study is useful because it challenges the idea that communication simply accelerates crowd consensus.

items.questionAndWhy: Why do coding agents succeed or fail when given the same scientific task? Model selection may matter less than the information, time, verification tools, and other conditions in which the model operates.
items.whatTheyDid: Wiedmann and colleagues tested five configuration dimensions on four scientific tasks requiring agents to find and operate published specialist models. They analyzed over 18,000 execution trajectories, varying task information, reasoning instructions, verification, time budgets, and language-model backbones.
items.whatTheyFound: About 54% of outcome variance arose from repeated runs with the same configuration. The information provided to an agent had the largest configuration effect. More time helped conditionally, and telling an agent to verify did little to change verification behavior; providing a dedicated verification tool changed it substantially. The benchmark covers four tasks, not every agent use case.
items.whatItMeans: Agent TEVV should compare complete configurations and repeated runs. Supplying the right evidence and an actual verification mechanism may be more effective than upgrading a model or adding instructions that merely request more careful reasoning.
items.streamTitle: Agent setup mattered more than model size in a scientific workflow benchmark
items.streamSummary: An arXiv benchmark varied instructions, information, verification, time limits, and model backbone across four scientific coding-agent tasks and released more than 18,000 trajectories. Roughly 54% of measured outcome variance came from repeating the same configuration, and the information supplied to agents mattered more than model size or time budget. Asking agents to verify had little effect, whereas giving them a dedicated verification tool altered their behavior. The evidence is limited to these tasks, but it reinforces that reliable agents are engineered systems, not just language models.

items.questionAndWhy: How can a rapidly expanding research field identify experts and related topics across institutions without relying only on citations or coauthor networks? This is also a problem for multidisciplinary research discovery.
items.whatTheyDid: Foppiano and colleagues used OpenAlex to collect 189,581 battery-related works. They combined coarse research concepts with LLM-extracted keyphrases, weighted descriptors by recency and authorship role, computed author similarities, and serialized the resulting graph as RDF linked to Wikidata.
items.whatTheyFound: The prototype produced browsable topical researcher profiles and similarity maps; it was designed for exploration rather than validated prediction of future collaboration. About 30% of source records lacked abstracts, and inherited author-disambiguation and affiliation errors limit reliability. The displayed network focused on a selected author subset.
items.whatItMeans: The portable method is especially useful for PSYWERX research discovery: combine controlled concepts, extracted terms, persistent identifiers, provenance, and time-aware weights. Missing metadata and identity reconciliation should remain visible rather than hidden by a polished interface.
items.streamTitle: An OpenAlex knowledge graph mapped 189,581 battery papers into searchable research expertise
items.streamSummary: A new paper demonstrates a cross-institutional research knowledge graph built from 189,581 battery-related publications in OpenAlex. The system combines broad bibliographic concepts with fine-grained keyphrases, weights topics by publication recency and authorship, and exposes researcher similarities through an RDF/Wikidata-linked interface. It offers a reusable architecture for finding expertise and adjacent topics without depending exclusively on coauthorship. However, about 30% of publications lacked abstracts, and inherited author-identity errors can distort similarity. The current demonstration supports discovery, not reliable prediction of future collaborations.

items.questionAndWhy: Can air defenders coordinate radar, visual identification, and different manufacturers’ interceptor drones quickly enough when the time to respond may be seconds?
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters observed a late-September Dutch airbase demonstration by Intelic of its Nexus software. Radar and other sensors flagged a mock hostile drone, an observation drone checked it using image recognition, and a human authorized launch of an AI-guided interceptor. Intelic holds a €30 million Dutch defense contract and says Nexus is being rolled out in Ukraine.
items.whatTheyFound: The demonstration showed integrated detection, verification, and engagement across different equipment. Intelic says automation can save valuable time, but public material does not quantify detection accuracy, identification errors, interoperability failures, or battlefield effectiveness. The launch authorization in the observed trial remained human.
items.whatItMeans: This is a concrete shift from optimizing single drones toward an integrated decision chain. Useful follow-up measures include sensor-to-shooter delay, identification accuracy, interoperability, override behavior, communications resilience, and successful engagements—not just whether components can be connected.
items.streamTitle: Dutch software linked multiple drone sensors and interceptors into one air-defense workflow
items.streamSummary: In a Dutch airbase trial observed by Reuters, Intelic’s Nexus software brought radar detections, camera and reconnaissance-drone verification, and an AI-guided interceptor into one command interface. A human made the final launch decision. The firm has a €30 million Dutch defense contract and says the system is being deployed in Ukraine to connect equipment from different suppliers. The trial demonstrates workflow integration rather than combat effectiveness: public figures for false identification, engagement success, latency savings, and degraded-network performance are absent. Those measures will determine the practical value of the system.

items.questionAndWhy: What happens when wartime drone attacks move from conventional infrastructure into cloud and AI computing hubs? The relevant outcome is both physical damage and the continuity of services that depend on the facility.
items.whatTheyDid: Yandex reported that drones struck its Sasovo data center on October 8, causing a fire and suspension of site operations. Reuters reviewed Yandex’s customer notice about a power problem in one cloud zone and reports of online disruptions. Sasovo hosts tens of thousands of servers.
items.whatTheyFound: Yandex said essential consumer services were unaffected, while some customers experienced power and service problems. The full damage, duration of disruption, and impact on AI training infrastructure were not disclosed. Reuters described this as the first major reported strike on a Russian data hub during the war.
items.whatItMeans: The case makes digital infrastructure an explicit wartime resilience target. Assess service continuity, restoration time, replication across zones, and compute dependencies separately from physical facility damage; the event does not by itself establish a lasting AI-capacity loss.
items.streamTitle: A drone strike halted a major Yandex data center while core services reportedly remained online
items.streamSummary: Yandex said a drone strike on its Sasovo data center caused a fire and suspended operations at the facility, which houses tens of thousands of servers. Affected cloud customers were directed toward other zones, while the company reported that core consumer services remained available. The extent of hardware damage and any effect on the site’s AI supercomputing resources were not disclosed. The strike extends wartime infrastructure risk to a major Russian data hub and illustrates why redundancy, service continuity, recovery time, and physical damage must be assessed separately.

items.questionAndWhy: Is Russia shifting covert activity from broad disruption toward Western factories that directly supply Ukraine? Analysts must distinguish an intelligence assessment of intent from independently measured strategic effect.
items.whatTheyDid: At an October 7 security conference, an official of Denmark’s domestic security service PET described reported sabotage against Danish defense suppliers and a recruitment pattern using Telegram and low-level paid reconnaissance tasks that can escalate into sabotage. Reuters reported the official’s account and Russia’s denial.
items.whatTheyFound: PET assessed that Russia had increased actual operations since early summer after broader efforts failed to stop NATO support for Ukraine. The Russian embassy rejected the allegation. Specific incidents and causal evidence of the asserted strategic shift were not fully disclosed publicly.
items.whatItMeans: This is relevant to coercion and organizational resilience, but the observed incidents, actor attribution, assessed objectives, and measured impact on production must remain distinct. Recruitment pathways and supply-chain vulnerability are useful follow-up research areas.
items.streamTitle: Danish intelligence says sabotage against Ukraine-linked defense production has intensified
items.streamSummary: Denmark’s domestic intelligence service says sabotage operations are increasingly targeting companies that supply Ukraine rather than aiming only at broad disruption. An official described the recruitment of low-level proxies through social platforms, sometimes beginning with simple reconnaissance before escalating. The service assesses that earlier tactics failed to deter NATO support and that weapons production is now a higher priority. Russia denies the accusations. This is an intelligence assessment, not an independently demonstrated account of Moscow’s intent or sabotage effectiveness, but it raises concrete concerns about defense-industrial security and proxy recruitment.

items.questionAndWhy: Do people who screen positive for ADHD symptoms benefit from the same charts and visual cues as other users, and does subjective preference reliably reveal which format helps them perform?
items.whatTheyDid: Khan and colleagues ran controlled information-processing tasks with 70 university students, 30 screening positive and 40 negative on the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale. They compared eight formats, including plain and highlighted text, bar charts, infographics, pictographs, and AI-modified text, using speed-accuracy measures and participant preferences.
items.whatTheyFound: Visualization effects differed significantly by screening group. Plain text, highlighted text, and bar charts with images generally performed better, whereas detailed infographics and AI-modified text were especially poor in the positive-screen group. Preferred formats did not always produce the best observed performance. The screening tool is not a clinical ADHD diagnosis.
items.whatItMeans: Design teams should test accessibility through task performance as well as preference surveys. A polished or AI-simplified presentation is not automatically easier to use, and performance differences from a small screened sample should not be treated as universal design rules.
items.streamTitle: Detailed infographics and AI-rewritten text performed poorly for students screening positive for ADHD symptoms
items.streamSummary: A controlled study of 70 university students compared eight ways of presenting information, including text, charts, infographics, and AI-modified wording. Thirty students screened positive for ADHD symptoms. The best-performing formats were relatively simple, while detailed infographics and AI-modified text were associated with substantially poorer performance in the positive-screen group. Reported preferences sometimes diverged from measured speed and accuracy. The sample was small, and a positive screening result is not an ADHD diagnosis, but the study shows why digital accessibility should be tested behaviorally rather than inferred from appearance or user preference alone.

items.questionAndWhy: How much real clinical evidence supports AI systems making real-time recommendations during operations, and are auditability, oversight, and equity being evaluated alongside technical feasibility?
items.whatTheyDid: Parikh and colleagues searched five databases covering 2010 to July 2026 and screened 3,020 records for prospective, intraoperative AI decision support. Five eligible studies were identified: one published feasibility study and four ongoing trial or registry protocols. The authors also mapped reporting against a proposed seven-domain Ethics-Implementation Scorecard.
items.whatTheyFound: Only one study had completed clinical results, from five analyzed patients; the others had no published outcomes. None of the five reported comprehensive audit logging, algorithm update procedures, or subgroup performance analysis. The proposed scorecard is illustrative, not a validated readiness or regulatory instrument.
items.whatItMeans: This is a useful example of the gap between prototype capability and evidence of safe deployment. Evaluation should capture model versions, clinician override behavior, decision logs, subgroup performance, and actual patient outcomes—not merely successful integration into an operating-room workflow.
items.streamTitle: A review found only one completed prospective study of AI decision support during surgery
items.streamSummary: A scoping review screened 3,020 records on AI decision support used during surgery and found only five eligible prospective efforts. Just one had published clinical feasibility results, based on five patients; the other four were registered or ongoing studies without reported outcomes. None described comprehensive decision logging, model-update procedures, or subgroup-performance analysis. The authors proposed a conceptual ethics and implementation scorecard, but did not validate it as a regulatory tool. The review underscores how quickly technical systems can advance ahead of prospective effectiveness, human-oversight, and auditability evidence.
